translation_updates.summary: Process philosophy is an approach in philosophy, centered on ontology and metaphysics, that identifies processes, changes, or shifting relationships as fundamental and posits transient occasions of change or becoming as the most fundamental things of the ordinary everyday real world. Based on the premise that being is dynamic, it opposes the substance metaphysics that has been the dominant research paradigm in the history of Western philosophy since Aristotle; in the Western tradition it is Heraclitus of Ephesus (born ca. 560 B.C.E.) who is commonly recognized as the founder of the process approach. The term is primarily associated with the work of Alfred North Whitehead and Charles Hartshorne, and in 1929 Whitehead produced the most famous work of process philosophy, Process and Reality. It is a complex and highly diversified field that is not tied to any school, method, position, or even paradigmatic notion of process, and it remains a research paradigm currently in use all around the world.

Charles Hartshorne (1897–2000) was an American philosopher who concentrated primarily on the philosophy of religion and metaphysics, but also contributed to ornithology. He is considered by many philosophers to be one of the most important philosophers of religion and metaphysicians of the twentieth century; he developed the neoclassical idea of God and produced a modal proof of the existence of God that was a development of Anselm of Canterbury's ontological argument. He is also noted for developing Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy into process theology, and he and Whitehead are regarded as the chief exponents of process theism. Most of the major elements of his philosophy were already apparent by the time he became familiar with Whitehead's thought, however, and it is a mistake to style him as Whitehead's disciple, since he departed from the older philosopher on a number of points.
